3: This experiment was undertaken to examine the sensory and nutritional quality of idli prepared from three aromatic rice landraces of West Bengal together with one non-aromatic check. The experiment was laid out in a two-factor completely randomised design with three replications and was repeated in two years. Factor A was variety, namely Gobindabhog (G), Radhunipagal (R), Kalojira (K) and the non-aromatic check Dudeshwar (D); Factor B was product, namely plain idli (I), idli fortified with carrot extract (CI) and idli fortified with beet extract (BI). This yielded twelve treatment combinations, designated DBI, DCI, DI, GBI, GCI, GI, KBI, KCI, KI, RBI, RCI and RI. Each parameter is treated in turn, the findings being presented first under Result and their interpretation under Discussion.
5: The two years of data were combined only after the error variances had been tested by the Bartlett chi-square test. The test proved non-significant for most characters, demonstrating that the error variances of the two years were comparable and that the data could legitimately be pooled. It was significant only for manganese, ash, PGI and springiness; for these four characters an Aitken transformation was applied prior to the analysis of variance, and the transformed means were used for testing significance.
6: The coefficient of variation fell below 3 per cent for most characters. It was lowest for calcium (0.20 per cent), total phenol and total antioxidant activity (0.34 per cent each), and highest for fat (15.91 per cent), resilience (11.71 per cent), copper (9.65 per cent) and anthocyanin (9.63 per cent).
7: The variety and product interaction was highly significant for most of the nutritional, mineral, colour and textural characters. It proved non-significant only for taste, texture, appearance, cooking quality and overall acceptability.
8: In the tables that follow, the values for the two years and the pooled value of the twelve treatment combinations are given as mean plus or minus standard deviation. The annual values are means of three replications and the pooled values means of six observations. The standard error of the mean, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level and the coefficient of variation are given beneath each table. Pooled means followed by the same letter do not differ significantly at the 5 per cent level. Each table is followed by a figure presenting the pooled means, in which the vertical bars denote the standard error of the mean and the letters above the bars the groupings at the 5 per cent level.
19: Amylose content (Table 4.1 and Fig. 4.1) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in DI (16.75 per cent), followed by KI (16.25 per cent), and lowest in RBI (9.78 per cent). Among the products the mean value was 15.13 in the plain product, 13.44 in the carrot fortified product and 10.10 in the beet fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (13.72) and lowest in Radhunipagal (11.14).
20: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.40, with a coefficient of variation of 2.73 per cent.
22: The most probable basis of the decline in amylose from the plain to the beet fortified product is a combination of simple dilution and enzymatic loss. The vegetable extract replaces a proportion of the rice and black gram solids, so that the amylose concentration of the batter falls in proportion to the quantity of extract added, an effect reported wherever vegetable purees are incorporated into cereal formulations (Sharma et al., 2012; Chhikara et al., 2019). Beyond this, the amylolytic microflora developing during the overnight fermentation hydrolyses a proportion of the linear amylose chains, amylose being more readily attacked by bacterial alpha-amylase than the branched amylopectin (Steinkraus, 1997; Iyer and Ananthanarayan, 2008; Nout, 2009). The importance of this fraction resides in the fact that amylose governs the extent of retrogradation and therefore the firmness of the cooled product (Juliano, 1992; Copeland et al., 2009). All twelve combinations fall within the low-amylose class of Juliano (1971, 1992), which accounts for the characteristically soft, moist eating quality of idli prepared from these small-grained landraces (Singh et al., 2000; Bhattacharya, 2011). The unequal magnitude of the decline in the different varieties, which generated the significant interaction, is attributable to varietal differences in granule structure and in the accessibility of amylose to enzymatic attack (Singh et al., 2003; Champagne, 2004). Kaviyaselvan et al. (2026) recorded a comparable range of amylose in idli prepared from ten rice cultivars with and without pearl millet and likewise found the value to be governed jointly by cultivar and by the composition of the batter.
31: Starch content (Table 4.2 and Fig. 4.2) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in DI (51.66 per cent), followed by KI (48.76 per cent), and lowest in GBI (24.05 per cent). Among the products the mean value was 47.63 in the plain product, 34.83 in the carrot fortified product and 26.23 in the beet fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Dudeshwar (38.51) and lowest in Gobindabhog (33.51).
32: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.50, with a coefficient of variation of 1.20 per cent.
34: The probable basis of the marked decline in starch on fortification is again the dilution of the rice and black gram base by the added extract, together with microbial utilisation of starch during fermentation. Beetroot and carrot carry very little starch of their own, so that every gram of extract added to the batter displaces an equivalent quantity of rice solids (Sharma et al., 2012; Singh and Hathan, 2014; Chhikara et al., 2019). The lactic acid bacteria and yeasts of the idli batter, chiefly Leuconostoc mesenteroides and Lactobacillus species, secrete amylases that hydrolyse starch to fermentable sugars during the overnight leavening period, which accounts for a further measurable loss (Mukherjee et al., 1965; Steinkraus et al., 1967; Soni and Sandhu, 1990; Iyer and Ananthanarayan, 2008). The higher starch content of the non-aromatic check relative to the three aromatic landraces is a varietal character and accords with Verma and Srivastav (2017), who reported a lower carbohydrate load in aromatic Indian rices than in non-aromatic rices, and with the general observation that starch content varies widely between rice genotypes (Champagne, 2004; Bhattacharya, 2011).
43: Total carbohydrate (Table 4.3 and Fig. 4.3) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in DI (60.21 per cent), followed by GI (58.20 per cent), and lowest in KBI (40.91 per cent). Among the products the mean value was 56.02 in the plain product, 47.98 in the carrot fortified product and 42.82 in the beet fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Dudeshwar (52.03) and lowest in Kalojira (46.52).
44: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.48, with a coefficient of variation of 0.86 per cent.
46: Total carbohydrate tracked starch closely, starch constituting by far its largest fraction in a rice-based food, so that the probable basis of its decline is the same dilution and fermentative loss described for starch (Steinkraus, 1997; Iyer and Ananthanarayan, 2008; Chhikara et al., 2019). A proportion of the decline may further be attributed to the conversion of carbohydrate to carbon dioxide and organic acids during leavening of the batter, a loss unavoidable in any naturally fermented cereal product (Soni and Sandhu, 1990; Blandino et al., 2003; Poutanen et al., 2009). The consistently higher values of the non-aromatic check reflect a genuine varietal difference in grain composition and accord with the comparison of aromatic and non-aromatic Indian rices made by Verma and Srivastav (2017) and with the values compiled for Indian cereals by Gopalan et al. (2004).
55: Total soluble sugar (Table 4.4 and Fig. 4.4) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in RBI (3.83 per cent), followed by DBI (3.67 per cent), and lowest in RI (0.53 per cent). Among the products the mean value was 3.35 in the beet fortified product, 2.47 in the carrot fortified product and 0.59 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Dudeshwar (2.42) and lowest in Gobindabhog (1.73).
56: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.04, with a coefficient of variation of 1.71 per cent.
58: Total soluble sugar behaved in precisely the converse manner to starch, and two mechanisms acting in the same direction account for this. First, beetroot is exceptionally rich in free sucrose, glucose and fructose, so that the addition of its extract introduces a large quantity of soluble sugar directly (Singh and Hathan, 2014; Chhikara et al., 2019); carrot likewise carries appreciable free sugars, though less than beetroot (Sharma et al., 2012). Second, the amylases produced by the fermenting microflora hydrolyse a proportion of the rice starch into maltose and glucose, so that the sugar removed from the starch fraction reappears in the soluble sugar fraction (Mukherjee et al., 1965; Iyer and Ananthanarayan, 2008; Ganzle, 2014). A comparable rise in reducing sugars during the fermentation of cereal batters has been reported by Blandino et al. (2003) and, for idli specifically, by Ghosh and Chattopadhyay (2011). The rise in soluble sugar is nutritionally relevant, since it partly accounts for the higher predicted glycaemic index of the beet fortified treatments.
67: Resistant starch (Table 4.5 and Fig. 4.5) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in DCI (1.97 per cent), followed by DI (1.89 per cent), and lowest in KBI (1.02 per cent). Among the products the mean value was 1.69 in the carrot fortified product, 1.55 in the plain product and 1.34 in the beet fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Dudeshwar (1.83) and lowest in Kalojira (1.23).
68: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.04, with a coefficient of variation of 2.68 per cent.
70: The most probable basis of the higher resistant starch of the carrot fortified treatments is the combined contribution of added dietary fibre and retrograded amylose. Carrot carries a substantial quantity of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin, which are determined along with the resistant fraction and which additionally restrict enzyme access to the starch granule physically (Sharma et al., 2012; Slavin, 2013). The amylose liberated during steaming re-associates as the product cools and forms the retrograded RS3 fraction, a process well documented in cooked and cooled rice and other cereals (Englyst et al., 1992; Sajilata et al., 2006; Copeland et al., 2009). The lower values of the beet fortified treatments are accounted for by their very low amylose and high free sugar content, which leaves little material available for retrogradation (Singh and Hathan, 2014; Chhikara et al., 2019). This fraction is nutritionally important, since it escapes digestion in the small intestine and undergoes fermentation in the colon to short-chain fatty acids (Slavin, 2013).
79: Non-resistant starch (Table 4.6 and Fig. 4.6) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in DI (50.78 per cent), followed by KI (47.56 per cent), and lowest in GBI (23.57 per cent). Among the products the mean value was 46.66 in the plain product, 33.75 in the carrot fortified product and 25.49 in the beet fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Dudeshwar (37.18) and lowest in Gobindabhog (32.88).
80: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.52, with a coefficient of variation of 1.30 per cent.
82: Non-resistant starch is the readily digestible complement of the resistant fraction, so that the probable basis of its behaviour is simply that it tracks total starch. It was highest where the rice base was undiluted and lowest in the beet fortified treatments, which carried the least starch of all (Englyst et al., 1992; Sajilata et al., 2006). The gelatinisation occurring during steaming disrupts the granule structure and converts most of the starch into a rapidly digestible form, which is why this fraction predominates in all the treatments (Bemiller and Whistler, 2009; Copeland et al., 2009). Fermentation contributes further by partially hydrolysing the granule surface and increasing the accessible surface area (Iyer and Ananthanarayan, 2008; Ganzle, 2014). The values recorded here are comparable with those reported for other steamed and fermented cereal products (Blandino et al., 2003; Poutanen et al., 2009).
91: Predicted glycaemic index (Table 4.7 and Fig. 4.7) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KBI (75.08 PGI), followed by GBI (73.61 PGI), and lowest in RCI (58.46 PGI). Among the products the mean value was 73.53 in the beet fortified product, 65.19 in the plain product and 60.49 in the carrot fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (67.56) and lowest in Radhunipagal (64.53).
